entry: Island country in South Asia, separated from [[India]] by the [[Palk Strait]]. Formerly known as Ceylon, it has a population of 22 million. About 74% of the population are Sinhalese, who speak the [[Sinhala language]], and about 15% are Tamils who speak the Tamil language. Its executive and judicial capital is [[Colombo]], also its largest city; Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital. The earliest known Buddhist writings on the island, the [[Pali Canon]], date back to 29 BCE. The [[Portuguese Empire|Portuguese]] established a colony in the sixteenth century, and the British Empire ruled a colony on the island from the early 19th century until 1948, when it gained independence as the Dominion of Ceylon. Sri Lanka has the highest level of human development in South Asia and is a member of the [[Non-Aligned Movement]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Internal conflict in [[Sri Lanka]], 1983–2009, between the government and Tamil separatists. Beginning on July 23, 1983, it was an intermittent [[Insurgency|insurgency]] by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), led by Velupillai Prabhakaran, to create an independent Tamil state in the north-east of the island. The LTTE fought in response to discrimination and violent persecution of Sri Lankan Tamils, including [[Pogrom|pogroms]] in 1956, 1958, 1977, 1981 and 1983 carried out by Sinhalese mobs, often with state support. After a 26-year military campaign, the Sri Lankan military defeated the LTTE in May 2009. The UN estimated 80,000–100,000 deaths immediately after the war. The Sri Lankan state has faced global criticism over alleged [[War crime|war crimes]], and the LTTE was notorious for attacks on civilians, including suicide bombings.

Indian actress, cited as the first female superstar of Indian cinema. She worked in Telugu, Tamil, [[Hindi]], [[Malayalam]] and [[Kannada]] films over a career of over 50 years, often playing strong-willed women on screen while being reticent off screen. Her first starring Hindi role was in *Solva Sawan* (1979), followed by hits such as *Mr. India* (1987) and *Chandni* (1989). She returned to film with *English Vinglish* (2012). Her final film, *Mom* (2017), her 300th, earned her a posthumous National Film Award for Best Actress. She received the Padma Shri in 2013. Her death in a [[Dubai]] hotel was attributed to accidental drowning.

Largest city and summer capital of Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, in the disputed [[Kashmir]] region. It lies on the Jhelum River in the Kashmir Valley, known for houseboats, gardens and traditional handicrafts such as the Kashmir shawl. Founded in the 6th century according to the Rajatarangini, it was the most important capital of the valley under Hindu dynasties and a major center of learning. In the late 16th century it became part of the [[Mughal Empire]], whose emperors used it as a summer resort; Shalimar and Nishat are among its best-known gardens. It became the summer capital of the Dogra kingdom in 1846. The city was a flashpoint of violence during the 1990s and early 2000s insurgency. In 2019 it became the summer capital of a union territory after the former state's reorganization.

Indian mathematician known for work in mathematical analysis, [[Number theory|number theory]], infinite series and continued fractions. He developed his research in isolation before a 1913 correspondence with [[G. H. Hardy]] of the [[University of Cambridge]], who recognized his work as extraordinary and arranged for him to travel to Cambridge. Ramanujan independently compiled nearly 3,900 results, mostly identities and equations, many of them completely novel. These included the Ramanujan prime and the Ramanujan theta function, which opened new areas of research. He became one of the youngest Fellows of the Royal Society, the second Indian member, and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. Ill health, now believed to have been hepatic amoebiasis, forced his return to India in 1919, and he died at the age of 32. The lost notebook, containing discoveries from his final year, was rediscovered in 1976.

Malay Buddhist thalassocratic empire based on the island of [[Sumatra]], in present-day Indonesia, that influenced much of [[Southeast Asia]]. It was an important center for the expansion of [[Buddhism]] from the 7th to 11th century and the first polity to dominate much of western Maritime Southeast Asia. Its economy depended on trade, and its main foreign interest was lucrative trade agreements with [[China]] that lasted from the [[Tang dynasty]] to the [[Song dynasty]]. The earliest reference is the account of a Chinese monk, Yijing, who visited for six months in 671. Recent research suggests it was primarily a land-based polity, with fleets serving as logistical support. The kingdom may have disintegrated after 1025 following Chola raids on its ports. It was largely forgotten until the French historian George Cœdès formally postulated its existence in 1918.

City (pop., 2020: 14,329) and [[County (United States)|county]] seat of St. Johns County, on the Atlantic coast of northeastern [[Florida]]. Founded on September 8, 1565, by Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the contiguous United States. It was the capital of Spanish Florida for over 200 years and of British East Florida from 1763. The 17th-century Castillo de San Marcos and St. George Street, with over 30 historic houses and attractions, draw tourists. It has been a tourist attraction since the late 19th century.

Breed of very large working dog from the Western Alps, bred for rescue work by the hospice of the Great St Bernard Pass on the Italian-Swiss border. [[Switzerland]] is recognized as its country of origin. The hospice acquired its first dogs between 1660 and 1670. The most famous, Barry, reportedly saved somewhere between 40 and 100 lives, and his body is preserved in the Natural History Museum in [[Bern]]. Crossbreeding with Newfoundlands in the 1850s changed the breed's appearance, and its long fur froze in the Alpine snow, reducing its effectiveness as a rescue dog.

Luminous weather phenomenon in which [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] is created by a corona discharge from a rod-like object, such as a mast or spire, in an atmospheric electric field. The blue or violet glow, often with a hissing or buzzing sound, is most noticeable during [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]]. It is named after St. Erasmus of Formia (St. Elmo), patron saint of sailors, who regarded it with awe and sometimes as a good omen. It can warn of an imminent [[Lightning|lightning]] strike. In 1751, [[Benjamin Franklin]] hypothesized that a pointed iron rod would light up at its tip during a lightning storm.

Capital and largest city of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, on the eastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula. It spans 446.04 sq km (172.22 sq mi) and is the easternmost city in North America, excluding Greenland. Its name is attributed to a belief that John Cabot sailed into the harbor on the Nativity of John the Baptist, though this is most likely a legend. A Portuguese map of 1519 shows it as São João. The city played a role in the [[Seven Years' War]], the [[American Revolutionary War]] and the [[War of 1812]]. [[Guglielmo Marconi]] received the first transatlantic wireless signal there.

Large international river in North America, connecting the [[Great Lakes]] with the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic]]. It flows northeast from [[Lake Ontario]] to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, through Ontario and Quebec in Canada and New York in the United States, and forms part of the Canada–United States border. As the primary outflow of the Great Lakes Basin, it has the second-highest discharge of any river in North America, after the [[Mississippi River]], and the 16th-highest in the world. Its [[Estuary|estuary]] is often cited by scientists as the largest in the world. The river has long been a transportation route for Indigenous peoples and played a key role in the development of [[Montreal]] and [[Quebec City]]. The name dates from 1604, when Samuel de Champlain recorded it on a map.

System of rivers, locks, canals and channels in eastern [[Canada]] and the northern United States that lets oceangoing vessels travel from the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] to the [[Great Lakes]], as far inland as Duluth, Minnesota. It is named for the [[St. Lawrence River]] and legally extends from [[Montreal]] to [[Lake Erie]], including the Welland Canal. Proposals for a binational deep waterway were first made in the 1890s. Canada and the United States jointly built the seaway from 1954 to 1959, and it has since transported over 2.5 billion metric tons of cargo, mainly iron ore, coal, grain and petroleum products. It is administered by the St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation in Canada and the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation in the United States. Its [[Lock (water navigation)|locks]] bypass several rapids and dams along the river.

Independent city (pop., 2020: 301,578) in [[Missouri]], near the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers. Founded on February 14, 1764, by French fur traders Gilbert Antoine de St. Maxent, Pierre Laclède and Auguste Chouteau, it was named for King Louis IX of France and became the regional center of the French Illinois Country. The United States acquired it in 1804 as part of the [[Louisiana Purchase]]. A major port on the Mississippi River, it was the fourth-largest city in the country from 1870 until the 1920 census. It separated from St. Louis County in 1877, becoming an independent city. In 1904 it hosted the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, also known as the St. Louis World's Fair, and the Summer Olympics. Its metropolitan area, which extends into Illinois, had an estimated population of over 2.8 million. The 630-foot (192 m) Gateway Arch is among its main attractions.

Papal basilica of the Italian Renaissance in [[Vatican City]], an enclave within [[Rome]]. Construction of the present church began on April 18, 1506, and was completed on November 18, 1626, replacing an older basilica built in the fourth century by [[Constantine the Great]]. Designed principally by Donato Bramante, [[Michelangelo]] and Carlo Maderno, with the piazza and fittings by [[Gian Lorenzo Bernini]], it is the largest church in the world by interior measure. Catholic tradition holds that it is the burial site of [[Saint Peter]], the first bishop of Rome, and many popes, cardinals and bishops have been buried there since the early Christian period. The [[Pope|pope]] presides over liturgies that draw audiences of 15,000 to over 80,000 people. It is not a cathedral, because it is not the seat of a bishop.

French poet and critic, a major figure of [[Symbolism (movement)|Symbolism]]. His work anticipated and inspired [[Cubism]], Futurism, Dadaism and [[Surrealism]]. His early verse owed much to [[Charles Baudelaire]], while his later work explored the relation between content and form, including the arrangement of words and spaces on the page, as in his last major poem, *Un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard* (1897). Because the sound of the words matters as much as their meaning, his poetry is difficult to translate. [[Claude Debussy]]'s *Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune* (1894) was a free interpretation of his poem *L'après-midi d'un faune* (1876), and [[Maurice Ravel]] set his poems to music in *Trois poèmes de Mallarmé* (1913). He hosted weekly gatherings on Tuesdays at his home on the rue de Rome, known as *les Mardistes*, that included [[W. B. Yeats]] and [[Rainer Maria Rilke]].

Building in which working animals, especially [[Horse|horses]] or [[Ox|oxen]], are kept, usually divided into stalls. Stables may also include storage for equipment and feed. The American-style stable, called a [[Barn|barn]], has a door at each end and individual stalls inside. The world's oldest known horse stables, at Pi-Ramesses in Qantir, [[Ancient Egypt]], were established by [[Ramesses II]] (c. 1304–1213 BC). They covered approximately 182,986 square feet and could contain about 480 horses. Free-standing stables began to be built from the 16th century, placed near the house as an indicator of an owner's position in the community. The word is also used for the horses a building contains and, metaphorically, for a group of people under one manager, such as the artists a gallery represents.

Venue for mostly outdoor sports, concerts or other events, consisting of a field or stage surrounded by tiered seating. The word comes from the Greek *stadion*, a length of 600 human feet (180 m). The [[Ancient Olympic Games]] at Olympia originally consisted of a single sprint along one stadion. Greek stadia were built for foot races, while Romans built circuses for horse races and developed the amphitheater for gladiatorial contests. The oldest known stadium was probably built around 2000 BC by the Indus Valley Civilization at Dholavira. The first modern stadiums were built in the late [[Victorian era]], as [[Association football|association football]] and [[Baseball|baseball]] grew in popularity. Most stadiums with a capacity of at least 10,000 are used for association football. Other popular stadium sports include [[American football|gridiron football]], [[Cricket]] and rugby, and many large venues also host concerts. Modern designs increasingly incorporate [[Sustainability|sustainability]] features.

Group of officers, enlisted personnel and civilians who serve the commander of a division or other large military unit in command and control. Also called a general staff, it plans and analyzes operations, gathers information, and relays, coordinates and supervises the execution of plans and orders, especially in complex, rapidly changing operations. Its functional groups include administration, [[Logistics|logistics]], operations, intelligence and training. A centralized staff gives tighter top-down control but requires a larger headquarters, while a decentralized staff improves situational focus and the speed of local action. Most [[NATO]] nations, including the United States, use the Continental Staff System, which originated with [[Napoleon]]'s military. The Commonwealth Staff System, used by most of the Commonwealth, has its origin in the British military.

Designated space for the performance of productions in [[Theatre|theater]] and the performing arts, serving as a space for [[Actor|actors]] and a focal point for the [[Audience|audience]]. The most common form in the West since the Italian Renaissance is the proscenium stage, in which the audience views one side through a large opening, the proscenium arch. A thrust stage extends into the audience on three sides, while in theater in the round the audience surrounds the stage on all four sides. Stages may be permanent features or temporary platforms, and may be constructed for a performance or adapted from another space. Stage floors were once raked upward to enhance perspective, but by the end of the 19th century most had level floors. Theaters with rope-operated flying systems, which were operated manually by stagehands, are known as hemp houses.

Technical skill in theatrical, film and video production, including constructing and rigging scenery, hanging and focusing lighting, fabricating [[Costume|costumes]], makeup, stage management, audio engineering and procuring props. Considered a technical rather than artistic field, it is primarily the practical implementation of a scenic designer's vision, and is distinct from the wider umbrella of scenography. One person may run a small production, but a modern Broadway show requires carpenters, painters, electricians, stagehands, stitchers and wigmakers. In ancient Greek theater, the mechane, a crane for lifting actors over the skene, supported the endings of plays in which a god suddenly resolved the storyline; it is the literal source of the phrase deus ex machina. By 1300, liturgical dramas in churches spread the message of [[Christianity]] using mansion stages, small wooden platforms representing places such as Heaven or Hell.

Iron-based alloy containing at least 10.5% [[Chromium|chromium]], which makes it resistant to [[Rust|rust]] and [[Corrosion|corrosion]]. The chromium forms a passive film that protects the metal and can self-heal in the presence of oxygen. Other elements, such as [[Molybdenum]] and [[Nickel]], may be added to enhance specific properties. Stainless steel is used in [[Cutlery|cutlery]], cookware, surgical instruments, major appliances, vehicles, large buildings and [[Chemical plant|chemical plants]]. Its biological cleanability is superior to copper and [[Aluminium|aluminum]], and comparable to glass, which has led to its use in pharmaceutical and food processing plants. The most common type, 304, has a tensile yield strength of around 210 MPa when annealed, rising to 1,050 MPa when cold worked. Melting points range from 1,325 to 1,530 °C. Martensitic, duplex and ferritic grades are magnetic, while austenitic grades are usually not. Types are labeled with an AISI three-digit number.

Structure of diagonally arranged horizontal steps that bridges a large vertical distance by dividing it into smaller ones. Alternatives include [[Elevator|elevators]], stairlifts, inclined moving walkways, [[Ladder|ladders]] and ramps. Each step is composed of a tread, the part stepped on, and a riser, the near-vertical element between steps. Stairs may run straight, change direction through 90° landings, or return on themselves with 180° landings, a common arrangement in multistory buildings. The concept is believed to be about 8,000 years old, and the oldest known spiral stairs date to the 400s BC. Standards vary by jurisdiction; the International Building Code requires uniform riser heights of 4 to 7 inches (102–178 mm).

1979 Soviet post-apocalyptic drama film directed by [[Andrei Tarkovsky]], loosely based on the 1972 novel *Roadside Picnic* by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky. A guide known as the Stalker leads a writer and a professor through a hazardous wasteland, the Zone, to a Room said to grant the innermost desires of anyone who enters. The film was shot over a year on film stock later found to be unusable and was almost entirely reshot. Released in May 1979, it received praise in the Soviet and Warsaw Pact press but only mixed reviews in the West.

American comic book writer, editor, publisher and producer, who was the primary creative leader of [[Marvel Comics]] for two decades. He rose through the ranks of Timely Comics, the family-run business that later became Marvel. With [[Jack Kirby]] and Steve Ditko, he co-created characters including [[Spider-Man]], the [[X-Men]], [[Iron Man]], Thor, the [[Hulk]], Ant-Man, the Fantastic Four, Black Panther and Doctor Strange. Introduced in the 1960s, these characters pioneered a more naturalistic approach in superhero comics. In the 1970s he challenged the restrictions of the Comics Code Authority. After retiring from Marvel in the 1990s, he remained its public figurehead, making cameo appearances in films based on Marvel properties. He received an executive producer credit on them, which made him the actor with the highest-grossing film total ever.

Art form in which a comic delivers humorous and satirical monologues on stage to a live audience, often interacting with the crowd. Routines consist of one-liners, stories, observations and shticks, and may employ props, music, impressions or [[Magic (illusion)|magic tricks]]. Stand-up draws on popular entertainments including [[Vaudeville]], minstrel shows, dime museums and humorist monologues such as [[Mark Twain]]'s 1866 touring show *Our Fellow Savages of the Sandwich Islands*. Charles Farrar Browne, known as Artemus Ward, is considered America's first stand-up comedian. Common genres include observational, anecdotal, deadpan, topical and [[Satire|satire]]. Performances take place in comedy clubs, festivals, bars, colleges and theaters, and during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] comics performed by video conferencing and on social media.
